previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. Johnson, a man with chronic systolic heart failure, atrial fibrillation, and a history of heavy alcohol use, was admitted after being found down intoxicated with complaints of left-sided chest pain. Initial evaluation ruled out acute cardiac event, pulmonary embolism, or aortic dissection via normal troponins, EKG, and CT imaging. The chest pain was determined to be musculoskeletal, reproducible on palpation and exacerbated by movement. He exhibited signs of alcohol withdrawal, managed with diazepam per CIWA protocol. His heart failure and hypertension were stable, with no decompensation; home medications including metoprolol, losartan, and furosemide were continued. He admitted non-compliance with Dabigatran, and was counseled on the importance of anticoagulation due to prior pulmonary embolism. He improved clinically, remained alert and coherent, and was discharged home in stable condition with instructions to monitor weight, continue all medications, and follow up with his primary care provider.

Brief Hospital Course:
History 
___ y/o M w/heart failure and angina presenting with acute RUQ 
and epigastric abdominal pain with nausea and vomiting. Patient 
was ruled out for an acute cardiac event. His abdominal pain was 
monitored with serial abdominal exams and blood work until 
resolution of his symptoms. He was also able to tolerate POs 
appropriately upon discharge.   

Active 
# RUQ abdominal pain: Patient presenting with first episode of 
RUQ pain. History of transaminitis and hyperbilirubinemia in 
past that had resolved and is now returned. AST>ALT consistent 
with alcoholic hepatitis. Pancreatitis is unlikely given normal 
lipase. RUQ ultrasound read is unremarkable for gallbladder 
disease at this time. Previous CT of the abdomen and pelvis in 
___ was unremarkable for liver disease. Patient's pain was 
well controlled. He was treated for likely gastritis/duodenitis 
given his previous history and onset of abdominal pain with 
continued EtOH abuse. He was transitioned from IV to PO pain 
medications and his diet was slowly advanced as tolerated. 

#Abnormal labs: Transaminitis elevated on admission but resolved 
over the course of his hospital stay and were felt to be related 
to alcohol ingestion. Indirect hyperbilirubinemia remained 
elevated through much of his hospital course. He was 
asymptomatic without evidence of jaundice or altered mental 
status. He was evaluated for possible hemolysis given acute on 
chronic anemia without evidence of active bleeding. However, 
while LDH was elevated, haptoglobin was normal  and peripheral 
smear was unremarkable suggesting hemolytic anemia was an 
unlikely cause. No clear current reason for hyperbilirubin but 
indirect bilirubin returned to normal at time of discharge, 
making ___ syndrome a possible explanation. 
Hemoglobin/hematocrit also returned to baseline at time of 
discharge.   

# EtOH abuse: Heavy alcohol use up until day of admission. EtOH 
level 130 on tox screen. There is no report of seizure with 
alcohol withdrawal in past. Patient placed on CIWA scale  
throughout hospitalization.
- Thiamine, folate, MVI daily 

# Chest pain: Patient has history of angina and a fib/a 
aflutter. States that his symptoms were exactly like his 
previous episodes of chest pain related to his angina.  
Asymptomatic throughout hospitalization with normal troponin and 
unchanged ECG x2. Likely his stable angina given symptoms now 
resolved. 
- Nitro SL PRN 

Inactive

- Continue home medications Zocor 10 and ASA 81mg daily

# GERD
- Continue Prilosec when able to tolerate POs.

- Continue home anticoagulation
